sentences.text: She found the shelves the following August, free-diving off the rocks at Agriolivado, which she was not supposed to do alone and did every day of every summer holiday of her childhood.
There is a ledge down there at about eight metres where the rock steps out and then goes on down into a slot too narrow for a person.
Iro had known that ledge since she was small.

What she had not known — because you cannot see it from above and because you have to be lying flat and looking sideways — was that under the overhang the rock has eight horizontal cracks in it, running back into the dark, one above the other, like a bookcase left out in the weather.
They were full.
She got about a second and a half of looking on the first dive, and eleven or twelve seconds on the fourth, and by the end of that August she had a fair idea.
Eight metres is not deep.
Eight metres is a nuisance: it is deep enough that you have perhaps twenty usable seconds on the bottom at thirteen years old, and shallow enough that you feel foolish for not having more.
She went down that ledge perhaps two hundred times that August.

She did it in the flat hour after lunch when the water goes glassy and the boats are in, and she did it with a mask that leaked, and she came up each time with about two shelves' worth of information in her head and lost half of it on the way to the surface.
A shelf of cups.
Not one kind — a tin mug, a china cup with no handle, a plastic beaker, a thing that might have been a chalice and was probably a trophy.
A shelf of things you hold up to your eye.
The compass was on it.
So were a pair of spectacles, a small brass telescope in bad condition, and something Iro is fairly sure was a broken camera.
A shelf of shoes, all of them singles.
A shelf of things with edges: knives, a plane blade, half a pair of scissors, a razor.

And so on, eight of them, down to the bottom shelf, which was the hardest to see and which held things Iro could never quite categorise until she was about fifteen and worked it out in the middle of a maths lesson: they were all things that had held something else.
A tin.
A wallet.
A box.
A shoe would have gone on the shoe shelf, but a purse went here.
She has never seen the octopus at the shelves.
She wants that stated plainly, because it is the weakest part of the whole account and because people always assume she has.
She has seen one on that ledge twice in thirty years, both times moving, neither time doing anything.
The den — if there is a den — is somewhere down the slot, and the slot goes into the rock at an angle and Iro has looked into it with a torch and seen nothing but rock.
The arrangement is not by material and it is not by size and it is not by age.
There is a plastic beaker two centimetres from a bronze cup.
It is by what the thing was for.
